messages.text: I’m just so tired of everything. It feels like I’m running on empty and there’s no point in refilling.

It sounds like you’ve been carrying a lot for a long time, and that exhaustion feels overwhelming. When you say there’s “no point,” do you mean you’re feeling hopeless about things improving? I want to understand how deep this fatigue goes for you so we can explore what might help. Are you also feeling emotionally drained, or is it more physical?
The future just feels like more of the same. I don’t see anything changing, and honestly, I don’t know if I care anymore.

That sense of numbness and hopelessness can be really heavy, and it often makes it difficult to imagine any reason to keep going. Sometimes these feelings can also point toward thoughts of not wanting to be alive—are you experiencing anything like that? It’s important to know so we can keep you safe and support you appropriately. Would you feel comfortable telling me if you’ve had thoughts of harming yourself?
I wouldn’t say I’m thinking about harming myself. I just… wouldn’t mind if I didn’t wake up, you know? It’s not dramatic—it’s just how it is.

I’m hearing something tender in what you just shared, and I want to pause with you here, [member’s name]. It sounds like you might be carrying a quiet heaviness about being here, and I’m wondering what that feels like for you right now. Could you tell me a bit more about what you meant when you said that?
It’s not that I want to do anything… it’s just that the idea of not being here feels like relief. Like the weight would finally stop. I know that sounds bleak, but it’s honest.

I hear the honesty in what you’re saying, [member’s name], and I want to pause with you in that feeling. It sounds like there’s a sense of relief in imagining the weight being gone, and I’m curious what it’s like to sit with that thought right now. Can you tell me more about what that relief represents for you?
It’s like… the relief isn’t about anything dramatic. It’s just the thought of not having to carry this anymore. Like finally being able to rest.

I’m hearing you, [member’s name], and it sounds like the “rest” you’re describing is about wanting the burden to ease. I’m wondering if that feeling comes with any urge to end your life, or if it’s more about longing for peace in another way. Could you share a bit more about what’s underneath that need for rest?
I probably just sound weak, like I can’t handle life as well as other people. I should be able to push through this, but I don’t even have the energy to pretend anymore.

You don’t sound weak to me, [member’s name] — what you’re describing takes a lot of courage to put into words. It seems like you’ve been pushing for a long time, and the energy to keep pretending just isn’t there right now. Is it okay if we explore what’s been draining you most, and see if there’s a way to lighten that load even a little?
Yeah, I’ve been pushing for years—through work, through losing her, through trying to be steady for everyone else. I just don’t know how to stop without falling apart.

It sounds like you’ve been carrying loss, responsibility, and pressure all at once, [member’s name], without much space to rest or be cared for yourself. Stopping can feel terrifying when everything has depended on you holding it together. Would it feel safe for you if we looked at small ways to let yourself pause without completely collapsing?
I do want to rest—God, I want to stop pretending—but I’m scared of what happens if I actually let go. It’s like I’m holding everything together by a thread, and if I relax, it all falls.

I can hear how tightly you’ve been holding on, [member’s name], and the fear that letting go might mean everything falls apart. I’m wondering—does that fear come with any thoughts of not wanting to be here anymore, or is it more about losing control of your life and responsibilities? Knowing that can help us find a way to give you some rest safely. Would you like to talk about what “letting go” would look like for you?
It’s not that I want to disappear—just that the idea doesn’t scare me like it should. Maybe that’s the real problem.

It takes a lot to share that, [member’s name], and it sounds like you’re noticing a shift in how you relate to the idea of not being here. That’s an important signal about how worn down you might be feeling. I’d like us to keep talking about this so you have space and support—would it feel okay to explore what’s been making life feel so heavy lately?

Last night I just lay there, staring at the ceiling. Couldn’t sleep—again. My skin was itching, my mind racing. I kept thinking about how long it’s been since I felt any real peace. Not since she passed. I used to be able to lose myself in a book, or a walk, or even just quiet. Now it’s all just… noise. And exhaustion.

Losing someone you love can strip away the things that once brought comfort, [member’s name], and it’s clear you’ve been living with that absence for a long time. The restlessness, the racing mind, the noise—those can be signs your grief and exhaustion are still pressing hard on you. Would you like to talk about her, or about what you miss most right now? Sometimes revisiting that connection can be a gentle way to start finding small pockets of peace again.

I keep coming back to that idea—not of dying, but of the weight finally being gone. It’s not about her, not really. It’s about not having to pretend I’m okay when I’m not. I just want to stop carrying it all.

I hear that, [member’s name]—it’s more about wanting relief from the strain and the pretending than about ending your life itself. That longing for the weight to lift makes sense, given how much you’ve been holding. Can we look together at what support might help you feel lighter without you having to carry it alone?

I don’t even know where to start. I’ve always been the one people come to—I don’t know how to say I’m the one who’s falling apart. And what would I ask for, anyway? “Help, I’m tired of existing”? That just sounds pathetic.

It’s not pathetic at all, [member’s name]—it’s human to reach a point where the load is too heavy to carry alone. Sometimes starting can be as simple as telling someone you trust that you’re struggling, without needing to explain everything perfectly. Would you like us to think through who in your life might be able to hear you and offer steady support right now?
I don’t know who I’d even talk to. My kids are trying, but they’ve got their own lives. My sister calls once a month. I just… don’t know how to be the one who needs help.

It can feel unsettling to step into that role, [member’s name], especially when you’ve always been the strong one. You don’t have to go from carrying everything to leaning entirely—sometimes it’s about small openings for connection. Could we explore together what a gentle first step might look like, even if it’s just telling one person you’re feeling worn down?
I don’t know… saying it out loud makes it real in a way I’m not sure I can handle. What if I break down and can’t stop? What if they expect me to fix it right away?

It’s understandable to fear that once you open the door, the feelings could flood in and overwhelm you, [member’s name]. You don’t have to fix it right away—sharing can be about letting someone witness your struggle without asking for solutions. Would it help if we thought about ways to prepare yourself for that conversation so you feel more in control of it?
That’s exactly it—I’m afraid if I start, I won’t be able to stop. And then what? I can’t afford to fall apart. People depend on me.

It sounds like holding yourself together feels essential because of those responsibilities, [member’s name], even though it’s exhausting. Sometimes allowing a safe, contained space to release a little of that pressure can keep you from breaking entirely. Could we explore what a “safe release” might look like for you, so you can let go without losing the structure you need?
What would that even look like—safe release? I don’t know how to do that without falling apart.

A safe release could be something small and structured, [member’s name], like setting aside a short time to express what you’re feeling—through writing, talking to a trusted person, or even physical movement—and then gently closing that space. It’s about letting some of the weight out without opening the floodgates all at once. Would you like us to think through one or two options that could feel manageable to try?
Writing it down maybe? I don’t know if I could say it out loud, but putting it on paper might be easier. Like it’s real, but not *heard*.

That could be a gentle starting point, [member’s name]—writing gives you a way to acknowledge your feelings without needing to face someone’s reaction right away. You can choose what to keep, tear up, or even stash somewhere safe, depending on what feels right. Would you like me to help you set up a short, manageable writing exercise for this?
I could try writing something tonight. I can’t promise I’ll keep it or show it, but I’ll try. It might help to get it out.

That sounds like a thoughtful step, [member’s name], and it’s okay if the writing stays just for you. Tonight, you might set a timer for 10 minutes and let yourself put down whatever rises in the moment, without worrying about structure or grammar. Afterward, notice how you feel and decide what to do with the pages based on what feels safest. Would you like a simple prompt to help you start?
What kind of prompt do you mean? Just… “how I’m feeling,” or something more specific?

It could be as simple as “What is the weight I’m carrying right now?” or “If I could set it down for a moment, what would that feel like?” You might also write to someone—real or imagined—about what you haven’t been able to say out loud. Would you like me to give you a few prompts so you can choose the one that feels easiest tonight?
Yeah, a few options might help. I’ll pick one that feels less… exposing. Just to start.

Here are a few gentle prompts, [member’s name]:  
1. “What would I want someone to understand about my life right now?”  
2. “If I could rest without consequences, what would that look like?”  
3. “The hardest thing about pretending I’m okay is…”  

Would you like me to also suggest a brief way to close your writing so you feel steady afterward?
Yeah, that might help—something to close it. I don’t want to just… leave it open.

To close your writing, you could end with a short grounding step—like jotting one small thing you’re grateful for, or something comforting in your immediate surroundings. You might also fold or place the pages somewhere specific, as a way of signaling “this is contained for now.” Would you like me to walk you through a simple grounding exercise you could use right after?
I could try that. Maybe just noting something simple—like the lamp being on, or the chair under me. Something real.

Yes, exactly, [member’s name]—naming something tangible anchors you in the present. After writing, look around and gently describe one or two things you see, feel, or hear, letting your body notice them. This can help signal to your mind that the expression is complete for now. Would you like me to remind you of this before you write tonight?
I’ll set a reminder on my phone for 8 PM. That should be quiet enough. Thanks for walking me through this.

That sounds like a thoughtful plan, [member’s name], and I’m glad you’re giving yourself that space. I’m here to support you as you try it, and we can talk afterward about how it felt. Would you like to check in tomorrow so you’re not carrying the experience alone?
Thanks, Dawn. I appreciate you not pushing, and still… getting it. I’ll reach out tomorrow.

I’m glad you feel understood, [member’s name], and I look forward to hearing from you tomorrow. You don’t have to carry this on your own. I hope tonight’s writing gives you even a small bit of relief.
